text: The retrieved literature on the hypothesis is thin. Van Bavel et al. (2020) argue that social and behavioural science should inform the COVID-19 pandemic response, which gives general backing to testing whether brief messages can shape public attitudes toward science. Ecker et al. (2022) review the psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction, which bears on whether any single message can move trust in science relative to a pure control. Berinsky et al. (2012) assess the internal and external validity of experiments run on Amazon Mechanical Turk, a relevant reference for an online randomised design. The main tension is between the expectation that messages can shift trust and Ecker et al.'s account of how resistant beliefs are to correction. Van Bavel et al. take the policy case for behavioural interventions as given, while Ecker et al. suggest that changing entrenched beliefs is hard. A design with 32 messages against a pure control can test whether any message departs from control, which speaks directly to this disagreement. Berinsky et al.'s validity concerns mean that any such effects would need to be read with the sample's limits in mind.

works.abstract: We examine the trade-offs associated with using Amazon.com 's Mechanical Turk (MTurk) interface for subject recruitment. We first describe MTurk and its promise as a vehicle for performing low-cost and easy-to-field experiments.
